claim: The juxtacellular recording and labeling technique was combined with optogenetics in freely moving mice to selectively target molecularly defined cell classes for in vivo single-cell recordings and morphological analysis.
source: In the present study, we combined the juxtacellular recording and labeling technique with optogenetics in freely moving mice. This allowed us to selectively target molecularly defined cell classes for in vivo single-cell recordings and morphological analysis.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The strategy was validated in the CA1 region of the mouse hippocampus by restricting Channelrhodopsin expression to Calbindin-positive neurons.
source: We validated this strategy in the CA1 region of the mouse hippocampus by restricting Channelrhodopsin expression to Calbindin-positive neurons.
evidence: The abstract describes the validation approach used in the study.

claim: Directly versus indirectly light-activated neurons could be readily distinguished based on the latencies of light-evoked spikes.
source: Directly versus indirectly light-activated neurons could be readily distinguished based on the latencies of light-evoked spikes, with juxtacellular labeling and post hoc histological analysis providing 'ground-truth' validation.
evidence: The abstract states that spike latencies can distinguish direct from indirect activation, validated by histology.

claim: Pyramidal cell identity is a key determinant for neuronal recruitment into the hippocampal spatial map.
source: pointing to pyramidal cell identity as a key determinant for neuronal recruitment into the hippocampal spatial map.
evidence: The abstract interprets the findings to suggest cell identity determines spatial map recruitment.

claim: Neural circuits consist of a large variety of neuronal elements with diversity encompassing morphological, genetic, physiological, and functional properties.
source: Since the seminal work of Ramón y Cajal it has become clear that neuronal circuits consist of a large variety of neuronal elements. Such diversity encompasses virtually all aspects of neuronal biology, including morphological, genetic, physiological, and functional properties.
evidence: This statement draws on established scientific knowledge about neuronal diversity.

claim: Major advances have been made toward the systematic classification of neuronal cell types.
source: Over recent years, major advances have been made toward the systematic classification of neuronal cell types (Ascoli et al., 2008; Scala et al., 2020; Tasic et al., 2016; Zeisel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on cell type classification.

claim: A combinatorial approach integrating morphological, molecular, electrophysiological, and functional properties is required for neuronal cell-type classification.
source: From these research lines, it has become increasingly clear that a combinatorial approach – integrating morphological, molecular, electrophysiological, and functional properties – is required for neuronal cell-type classification.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cited research on cell type classification.

claim: Current in vivo techniques for neural circuit analysis provide only limited information about the recorded neuronal elements.
source: Bridging this gap is a methodological challenge, since current in vivo techniques for neural circuit analysis – for example optogenetic tagging and Ca2+ imaging (Anikeeva et al., 2011; Ghosh et al., 2011; Lima et al., 2009) – provide only limited information about the recorded neuronal elements.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to work on optogenetic tagging and calcium imaging.

claim: Optogenetic tagging and calcium imaging methods largely rely upon the genetically restricted expression of Channelrhodopsin or calcium indicators via Cre driver lines.
source: These methods largely rely upon the genetically restricted expression of Channelrhodopsin (ChR2) or Ca2+ indicators – for example via Cre driver lines (Adesnik, 2018; Gafford and Ressler, 2016; Kravitz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations describing the use of Cre driver lines in optogenetics.

claim: In optogenetic tagging, recordings are performed with a dual optical and electrical probe (optrode) and short-latency spikes elicited upon illumination provide information about the identity of the recorded units.
source: In the case of 'optogenetic tagging', recordings are performed with a dual optical and electrical probe (referred to as 'optrode') and short-latency spikes elicited upon illumination provide information about the identity of the recorded units.
evidence: This describes the standard optogenetic tagging methodology.

claim: A limitation of optogenetic tagging is that cell types are defined by single features like genetic marker expression or projection target.
source: One limitation of this approach is that 'cell types' are defined by single features, like genetic marker expression or projection target.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the limitations of optogenetic tagging methods.

claim: Additional structural features like morphology, local and long-range axonal projections, and gene expression profiles are not accessible with optogenetic tagging and calcium imaging techniques.
source: Additional structural features – like morphology, local and long-range axonal projections, and gene expression profiles – are not accessible with these techniques, thereby making it difficult to map neuronal activity (assessed in vivo) to the multidimensional cell-type classification schemes (being developed in vitro).
evidence: This claim identifies specific limitations of current in vivo recording methods.

claim: The juxtacellular method allows recording of single neurons in awake behaving animals, along with post hoc morphological analysis and molecular phenotyping of the recorded cells.
source: For example, the juxtacellular method (Pinault, 1996; Pinault, 1994) allows recording of single neurons in awake behaving animals, along with post hoc morphological analysis and molecular phenotyping of the recorded cells (Averkin et al., 2016; Diamantaki et al., 2018; Katona et al., 2014; Lapray et al., 2012; Tang et al., 2014b; Valero et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations describing juxtacellular recording methods.

claim: A significant limitation of juxtacellular methods is that neurons are typically sampled by blind procedures, making it challenging to efficiently sample sparse neuronal elements within a given circuit.
source: However, a significant limitation of these methods is that neurons are typically sampled by 'blind' procedures; hence, recordings cannot be targeted to a predefined cell class, which makes it extremely challenging – if not impossible – to efficiently sample sparse neuronal elements within a given circuit.
evidence: This identifies a key limitation of traditional juxtacellular recording approaches.

claim: An approach combining single-cell identification techniques with optogenetic tagging has been developed to enable ChR2-assisted targeting of genetically defined cell classes.
source: To circumvent this limitation, an elegant approach has been recently developed by combining single-cell identification techniques with optogenetic tagging (Katz et al., 2013; Muñoz et al., 2014). This approach enabled ChR2-assisted targeting of genetically defined cell classes
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work combining these techniques.

claim: The combination of juxtacellular labeling and post hoc morphological/molecular analysis provides access to multidimensional neuronal features required for precise cell-type classification.
source: in addition, by means of juxtacellular labeling and post hoc morphological/molecular analysis, it also provided access to the multidimensional neuronal features required for precise cell-type classification (Muñoz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to work demonstrating this capability.

claim: The applicability of the single-cell opto-tagging method is limited to mechanically stable preparations (e.g., anesthetized or head-restrained animals), preventing structure-function analysis in freely moving animals.
source: In its current form however, the applicability of this method is limited to mechanically stable preparations (e.g., anesthetized or head-restrained animals), thereby preventing structure–function analysis in freely moving animals, engaged in ethologically relevant behaviors.
evidence: This identifies a limitation of the existing opto-tagging method.

claim: The study aimed to bridge the gap by combining the single-cell opto-tagging method with juxtacellular procedures established in freely moving mice.
source: In the present study, we aimed at bridging this gap by combining the single-cell opto-tagging method (Katz et al., 2013; Muñoz et al., 2014) with the juxtacellular procedures that we have recently established in freely moving mice (Diamantaki et al., 2018).
evidence: This states the main goal of the study with supporting citations.

claim: The approach enabled efficient targeting of juxtacellular recording and labeling to predefined, genetically tagged cell classes in awake animals engaged in natural exploratory behavior.
source: This approach enabled us to efficiently target juxtacellular recording and labeling to predefined, genetically tagged cell classes in awake animals, engaged in natural exploratory behavior.
evidence: This describes the capability achieved by the new method.

claim: The activity of place cells in the CA1 region is thought to contribute to the encoding of spatial and episodic experiences and form the neural basis of memory engrams.
source: During behavior, the activity of 'place cells' in this region (O'Keefe, 1976) is thought to contribute to the encoding of spatial and episodic experiences, and thus to form the neural basis of 'memory engrams' (Tonegawa et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational work on place cells and memory engrams.

claim: Despite its relatively simple organization, the CA1 has a remarkably diverse cellular composition.
source: Anatomically – despite its relatively simple organization – the CA1 has a remarkably diverse cellular composition.
evidence: This is a general statement about CA1 anatomy based on established knowledge.

claim: In vitro and in vivo work has distinguished more than 20 different morphofunctional interneuronal classes in the CA1.
source: In vitro and in vivo work has distinguished more than 20 different morphofunctional interneuronal classes (Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013; Freund and Buzsáki, 1998; Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to work classifying CA1 interneurons.

claim: Recent transcriptomic studies point to a complex heterogeneity among pyramidal neurons, with at least 15 classes identified based on gene expression data.
source: recent transcriptomic studies point to a seemingly complex heterogeneity among pyramidal neurons, with at least 15 classes being identified purely based on gene expression data (Yao et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to transcriptomic studies.

claim: It is unclear how distinct CA1 cell types contribute to neural activity during behavior.
source: At present it is unclear how these distinct cell types contribute to neural activity during behavior.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge about CA1 cell types.

claim: The anatomical location of CA1 neurons along the deep-superficial axis correlates with in vivo activity patterns.
source: Indeed, a growing body of evidence indicates that the anatomical location of the neurons along this axis correlates with in vivo activity patterns (Cohen et al., 2017; Danielson et al., 2016; Fattahi et al., 2018; Geiller et al., 2017; Li et al., 2017; Mizuseki et al., 2011; Sharif et al., 2021; Valero et al., 2015; for review, see Preston-Ferrer and Burgalossi, 2018; Soltesz and Losonczy, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies showing this correlation.

claim: Calbindin (Calb1) expression is selective for superficially located pyramidal neurons in CA1.
source: We thus took advantage of the expression of Calbindin (Calb1) – which is selective for superficially located pyramidal neurons
evidence: This is a known anatomical feature of CA1 pyramidal neurons.

claim: Calb1-negative pyramidal neurons were preferentially recruited into the place cell map while Calb1-positive pyramidal cells were only weakly spatially modulated.
source: We found that, while animals explored a familiar environment, Calb1-negative pyramidal neurons were preferentially recruited into the place cell map, while Calb1-positive pyramidal cells were only weakly spatially modulated.
evidence: This is the main experimental finding of the study.

claim: The data are consistent with the emerging idea of an asymmetric recruitment of CA1 pyramidal cell types into the hippocampal representation.
source: These data are thus consistent with the emerging idea of an asymmetric recruitment of CA1 pyramidal cells types into the hippocampal representation.
evidence: This interprets the findings in the context of existing hypotheses.

claim: Injections of AAV-CAG-flex-GFP in Calb1cre mice resulted in selective labeling of superficial pyramidal cells along with scattered putative interneurons located primarily within the stratum oriens.
source: As expected from the distribution of Calb1-positive neurons within the CA1 pyramidal layer, injections of AAV-CAG-flex-GFP in Calb1cre mice resulted in selective labeling of superficial pyramidal cells (Figure 1A) along with scattered, putative interneurons located primarily within the stratum oriens (not shown).
evidence: This describes the observed pattern of viral expression shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A representative light-responsive pyramidal neuron was located in the superficial pyramidal layer and its apical dendrite displayed a proximal branching point.
source: This neuron was located in the superficial pyramidal layer and its apical dendrite displayed a proximal branching point (see Figure 1C) – a characteristic morphological correlate of superficial CA1 pyramidal neurons (Bannister and Larkman, 1995; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes morphological features of a recorded neuron shown in Figure 1C, with citations supporting the interpretation.

claim: A proximal branching point of the apical dendrite is a characteristic morphological correlate of superficial CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: a proximal branching point (see Figure 1C) – a characteristic morphological correlate of superficial CA1 pyramidal neurons (Bannister and Larkman, 1995; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: A representative neuron was confirmed to be positive for the marker Calb1 as well as ChR2.
source: This neuron was confirmed to be positive for the marker Calb1 as well as ChR2 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes immunohistochemical confirmation shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Blue light pulses could reliably drive short-latency spikes (mean latency = 2.1 ± 0.12 ms) in a representative Calb1-positive neuron.
source: Indeed, blue light pulses could reliably drive short-latency spikes (mean latency = 2.1 ± 0.12 ms; Figure 1D, E) thus confirming the Calb1-positive identity of the recorded cell.
evidence: This reports quantitative data on spike latencies shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: 19 neurons were recorded and labeled in anesthetized mice.
source: Altogether, we recorded and labeled 19 neurons in anesthetized mice.
evidence: This reports the sample size for the anesthetized dataset.

claim: In all cases where short-latency spiking responses were observed (mean latency <4 ms), the neurons were confirmed to be Calb1-positive by immunohistochemical analysis (n = 10).
source: In all cases where short-latency spiking responses were observed (mean latency <4 ms; Figure 1F) the neurons were confirmed to be Calb1-positive by immunohistochemical analysis (n = 10), therefore validating our opto-tagging strategy.
evidence: This reports validation data with reference to Figure 1F.

claim: Seven additional nonresponsive neurons were juxtacellularly labeled and confirmed to be Calb1-negative pyramidal cells.
source: Seven additional nonresponsive neurons were also juxtacellularly labeled and confirmed to be Calb1-negative pyramidal cells (not shown).
evidence: This reports additional validation data for nonresponsive neurons.

claim: Two light-responsive, narrow-waveform neurons were recorded that were positive for Calb1 immunoreactivity and classified as putative Calb1-positive interneurons.
source: In two cases, we recorded the activity of light-responsive, narrow-waveform neurons (spike peak-to-trough <0.4 ms, see Ding et al., 2020; Preston-Ferrer et al., 2016) which were positive for Calb1 immunoreactivity, and were thus classified as putative Calb1-positive interneurons (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C; these neurons were not included in further analysis).
evidence: This describes recordings of interneurons with reference to supplementary figure and citations for classification criteria.

claim: One known challenge of optogenetic tagging experiments is to reliably distinguish directly versus indirectly excited neurons.
source: One known challenge of optogenetic tagging experiments is to reliably distinguish directly versus indirectly excited neurons (e.g., Beyeler et al., 2016; Zutshi et al., 2018).
evidence: This identifies a known methodological challenge with supporting citations.

claim: The short latency of light-responsive neurons together with post hoc validation by juxtacellular labeling provide strong support for direct light activation.
source: The short latency of our light-responsive neurons (Figure 1F) together with post hoc validation by juxtacellular labeling (Figure 1C), provide strong support for direct light activation.
evidence: This interprets the data from Figures 1C and 1F to support direct activation.

claim: AAV-CAG-ChR2-mCherry was injected in the CA3 of wild-type mice to obtain strong labeling of CA3 axon terminals (Schaffer collaterals) extending into the CA1 strata radiatum and oriens.
source: To this end, we injected AAV-CAG-ChR2-mCherry in the CA3 of wild-type mice (Figure 2A). By these means, we obtained strong labeling of CA3 axon terminals (Schaffer collaterals), extending into the CA1 strata radiatum and oriens (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: In a representative light-responsive CA1 pyramidal neuron, photostimulation at ~1.3 mW was sufficient for inducing suprathreshold spiking with lower efficiency and longer latencies (7.4 ± 0.8 ms) compared to directly light-activated neurons.
source: In this neuron, photostimulation at ~1.3 mW was sufficient for inducing suprathreshold spiking (Figure 2C), although with lower efficiency and longer latencies (7.4 ± 0.8 ms) as compared to the directly light-activated neurons (see Figure 1C–F).
evidence: This reports quantitative data on a representative neuron shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The response latencies of indirectly light-activated CA1 neurons were significantly longer than those of directly light-activated CA1 Calb1-positive cells (direct: 2.7 ± 0.3 ms, n = 10; indirect: 7.0 ± 1.8 ms, n = 11; p = 0.0010).
source: At the population level, the response latencies of indirectly light-activated CA1 neurons were significantly longer than those of directly light-activated CA1 Calb1-positive cells (direct light activation, mean latency = 2.7 ± 0.3 ms, n = 10; indirect light activation, mean latency = 7.0 ± 1.8 ms, n = 11; p = 0.0010; Figure 2E)
evidence: This reports statistical comparison of latencies with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: The longer response latencies of indirectly light-activated CA1 neurons further validate the latency-based criteria for cell-type classification.
source: thereby further validating our latency-based criteria for cell-type classification.
evidence: This interprets the latency data as validation of the classification method.

claim: The hippocampal mossy fiber synapse is among the strongest and most reliable connections in the nervous system.
source: To this end, we performed a subset of experiments on the hippocampal mossy fiber synapse, which is among the strongest and most reliable connections in the nervous system (Henze et al., 2002; Neubrandt et al., 2018; Vyleta et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing mossy fiber synapses.

claim: ChR2 was selectively expressed in dentate gyrus granule cells by injecting AAV-hSyn1-flex-ChR2-mCherry (or AAV-hSyn1-flex-oChIEF-TdTomato) in the dentate gyrus of Calb1cre mice, resulting in strong labeling of presynaptic mossy fiber terminals extending into the CA3 field.
source: We selectively expressed ChR2 in dentate gyrus granule cells by injecting AAV-hSyn1-flex-ChR2-mCherry (or AAV-hSyn1-flex-oChIEF-TdTomato) in the dentate gyrus of Calb1cre mice (Figure 2F). By these means, we obtained strong labeling of presynaptic mossy fibers terminals, extending into the CA3 field (Figure 2F, G).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach shown in Figures 2F and 2G.

claim: In a nonresponsive CA3 neuron, no spiking activity was observed upon light illumination, but a prominent light-induced facilitation of local field potential amplitude was observed, consistent with facilitation of neurotransmitter release at mossy terminals.
source: In the first neuron, no spiking activity was observed upon light illumination; however, a prominent light-induced facilitation of local field potential amplitude was observed – consistent with the known facilitation of neurotransmitter release at mossy terminal (Capogna, 1998; Vyleta et al., 2016; Zucca et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes observations from a representative neuron with citations supporting the interpretation.

claim: In a responsive CA3 neuron, photostimulation was sufficient for inducing suprathreshold spiking whose probability increased as a function of stimulus number, consistent with presynaptic facilitation of mossy inputs.
source: In the second neuron, photostimulation was sufficient for inducing suprathreshold spiking (Figure 2H), whose probability increased as a function of stimulus number, consistent with presynaptic facilitation of mossy inputs.
evidence: This describes observations from a representative neuron shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The response latencies of synaptically activated CA3 neurons (mean latency = 8.1 ± 2.4 ms, n = 7) were significantly longer than that of directly light-activated CA1 Calb1-positive cells.
source: Notably, the response latencies of synaptically activated CA3 neurons (mean latency = 8.1 ± 2.4 ms, n = 7) were significantly longer than that of directly light-activated CA1 Calb1-positive cells (Figure 2J).
evidence: This reports quantitative comparison of latencies with reference to Figure 2J.

claim: The dataset shows the technical feasibility of combining the opto-juxtacellular approach for single-cell recording, labeling, and presynaptic input manipulations.
source: Altogether, this dataset shows the technical feasibility of combining the opto-juxtacellular approach for single-cell recording, labeling, and presynaptic input manipulations.
evidence: This summarizes the technical validation achieved in the study.

claim: The longer spike latencies in indirectly activated neurons compared to directly activated ones further corroborate the validity of the latency-based opto-tagging approach.
source: Moreover, the longer spike latencies in indirectly activated neurons compared to the directly activated ones (Figure 2J) further corroborate the validity of our latency-based opto-tagging approach.
evidence: This interprets the latency data from Figure 2J as validation of the method.

claim: Animals were implanted with miniaturized components and a 50-μm-core optic fiber was inserted within the glass electrode for recordings in freely moving mice.
source: Animals were implanted with miniaturized components (see Figure 3A; Diamantaki et al., 2018) and a 50-μm-core optic fiber was inserted within the glass electrode.
evidence: This describes the recording configuration shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The use of a reversible fiber fixation strategy together with a mechanical micropositioning system allowed multiple recording/opto-tagging trials within individual animals.
source: The use of a reversible fiber fixation strategy, together with a mechanical micropositioning system (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1; details in Materials and Methods) allowed us to perform multiple recording/opto-tagging trials within individual animals.
evidence: This describes a technical feature enabling repeated recordings.

claim: All neurons included in the study displayed low firing rates (<10 Hz; average firing rate, 2.16 ± 2.06 Hz; n = 54) and often fired complex spikes (average burst index, 0.28 ± 0.18, n = 45).
source: All neurons included in the present study displayed low firing rates (<10 Hz; average firing rate, 2.16 ± 2.06 Hz; n = 54) and often fired complex spikes (average burst index, 0.28 ± 0.18, n = 45) – features classically associated with principal cell identity (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; Ranck, 1973).
evidence: This reports quantitative characterization of recorded neurons with citations supporting the interpretation.

claim: Low firing rates and complex spike firing are features classically associated with principal cell identity.
source: features classically associated with principal cell identity (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; Ranck, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classic studies on hippocampal neurons.

claim: All histologically identified neurons were classified as pyramidal neurons, confirming the electrophysiological classification criteria.
source: All histologically identified neurons were classified as pyramidal neurons (see Materials and Methods), thus further confirming our electrophysiological classification criteria.
evidence: This reports validation of classification criteria through histology.

claim: Neurons recorded in behaving mice were classified as Calb1-positive if short-latency spikes (<4 ms) were reliably evoked by the light pulse (n = 15).
source: As in the anesthetized dataset (Figure 1), neurons recorded in behaving mice were classified as Calb1-positive if short-latency spikes (<4 ms) were reliably evoked by the light pulse (n = 15; Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes the classification criteria applied to behaving animal data.

claim: In a subset of recordings, juxtacellular labeling was performed and the cytochemical identity of the recorded neuron was assessed via Calb1 immunoreactivity.
source: In a subset of recordings, juxtacellular labeling was performed and the cytochemical identity of the recorded neuron was assessed via Calb1 immunoreactivity (Figure 3C–H).
evidence: This describes validation procedures shown in Figures 3C-H.

claim: Neurons were classified as Calb1-negative neurons (n = 39) if they did not respond to the light stimulus or were located in the deep pyramidal layer and were negative for Calb1 expression.
source: Neurons were classified as Calb1-negative neurons (n = 39) if they did not respond to the light stimulus or were located in the deep pyramidal layer and were negative for Calb1 expression (see Materials and Methods).
evidence: This describes the classification criteria for Calb1-negative neurons.

claim: Two light-responsive, putative Calb1-positive interneurons were recorded that fired at high rates during exploration (>10 Hz average firing rates).
source: In two cases, we recorded from light-responsive, putative Calb1-positive interneurons, which fired at high rates during exploration (>10 Hz average firing rates; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–I; these neurons were not included in further analysis).
evidence: This describes recordings of interneurons shown in supplementary figure.

claim: During spatial exploration, Calb1-positive and Calb1-negative pyramidal cells displayed similar average firing rates (Calb1-positive: 2.17 ± 2.02 Hz, n = 15; Calb1-negative: 2.15 ± 2.10 Hz, n = 39; p = 0.86).
source: During spatial exploration, Calb1-positive and Calb1-negative pyramidal cells displayed similar average firing rates (Calb1-positive, 2.17 ± 2.02 Hz, n = 15; Calb1-negative, 2.15 ± 2.10 Hz, n = 39; p = 0.86)
evidence: This reports statistical comparison of firing rates between cell types.

claim: Calb1-positive and Calb1-negative pyramidal cells displayed similar tendency to fire spike bursts (Calb1-positive: 0.29 ± 0.21, n = 13; Calb1-negative: 0.29 ± 0.18, n = 32; p = 0.97).
source: and tendency to fire spike bursts ('burst index'; Calb1-positive, 0.29 ± 0.21, n = 13; Calb1-negative, 0.29 ± 0.18, n = 32; p = 0.97).
evidence: This reports statistical comparison of burst indices between cell types.

claim: Calb1-positive and Calb1-negative pyramidal cells differed remarkably in the degree of spatial modulation.
source: However, these two cell types differed remarkably in the degree of spatial modulation.
evidence: This summarizes the main finding about spatial modulation differences.

claim: The large majority of Calb1-negative neurons displayed spatially localized firing patterns that were homogeneously distributed over the available space.
source: While the large majority of Calb1-negative neurons displayed spatially localized firing patterns, which were homogeneously distributed over the available space (Figure 3I)
evidence: This describes the spatial firing patterns shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The spiking activity of Calb1-positive neurons was less spatially modulated.
source: the spiking activity of Calb1-positive neurons was less spatially modulated (Figure 3J)
evidence: This describes the spatial firing patterns shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Calb1-positive neurons conveyed significantly less spatial information (0.65 ± 0.35 bits/spike, n = 12) than Calb1-negative neurons (1.56 ± 0.79 bits/spike, n = 26; p = 0.0003).
source: Indeed, we found that Calb1-positive neurons conveyed significantly less spatial information (Calb1-positive, 0.65 ± 0.35 bits/spike, n = 12; Calb1-negative, 1.56 ± 0.79 bits/spike, n = 26; p = 0.0003)
evidence: This reports statistical comparison of spatial information content shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Calb1-positive neurons displayed a higher sparsity index (0.53 ± 0.15, n = 12) than Calb1-negative neurons (0.31 ± 0.17, n = 26; p = 0.0003), indicating a more diffuse firing pattern.
source: and displayed a higher sparsity index (Calb1-positive, 0.53 ± 0.15, n = 12; Calb1-negative, 0.31 ± 0.17, n = 26; p = 0.0003) (Figure 3K), indicating a more diffuse firing pattern compared to Calb1-negative cells.
evidence: This reports statistical comparison of sparsity shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Spatial firing in Calb1-positive neurons was significantly less stable than in Calb1-negative cells (mean correlation coefficient, Calb1-positive: 0.33 ± 0.35, n = 12; Calb1-negative: 0.68 ± 0.31, n = 26; p = 0.0019).
source: Indeed, in line with their weaker spatial tuning (Figure 3K), spatial firing in Calb1-positive neurons was significantly less stable than in Calb1-negative cells (mean correlation coefficient, Calb1-positive, 0.33 ± 0.35; n = 12; Calb1-negative, 0.68 ± 0.31; n = 26; p = 0.0019; see Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This reports statistical comparison of spatial stability shown in supplementary figure.

claim: The findings are in line with previous observations and indicate that in the dorsal CA1, place cells are preferentially contributed by deep (Calb1-negative) pyramidal neurons, while Calb1-positive neurons are only weakly spatially modulated.
source: Altogether, these findings are in line with previous observations (Danielson et al., 2016; Geiller et al., 2017; Mizuseki et al., 2011; Oliva et al., 2016; Sharif et al., 2021) and indicate that in the dorsal CA1, place cells are preferentially contributed by deep (Calb1-negative) pyramidal neurons, while Calb1-positive neurons are only weakly spatially modulated.
evidence: This interprets the findings in the context of previous work with supporting citations.

claim: The combination of extracellular recordings with optogenetic tagging has become a gold-standard approach for neural circuit dissection in freely behaving animals.
source: In freely behaving animals, the combination of extracellular recordings with optogenetic tagging (e.g., Anikeeva et al., 2011; Lima et al., 2009) has become a gold-standard approach for neural circuit dissection.
evidence: This describes the current state of the field with supporting citations.

claim: Cell-type identification in opto-tagging is indirect since it is inferred from the spiking responses to the light stimuli.
source: First, cell-type identification is indirect, since it is inferred from the spiking responses to the light stimuli.
evidence: This identifies a limitation of optogenetic tagging methods.

claim: Distinguishing directly versus indirectly light-activated neurons is often far from trivial, especially within networks with high recurrent connectivity.
source: While a number of criteria have been proposed for distinguishing directly versus indirectly light-activated neurons, this distinction is often far from trivial, especially within networks with high recurrent connectivity (Beyeler et al., 2016; Roux et al., 2014; Zutshi et al., 2018).
evidence: This identifies a challenge in optogenetic tagging with supporting citations.

claim: The reliability of optogenetic identification is complicated by the challenge of spike sorting during periods of highly synchronous activity, since the superimposition of multiple co-occurring spike waveforms can make the detection of individual spikes difficult and unreliable.
source: The reliability of optogenetic identification is further complicated by the challenge of 'spike sorting' during periods of highly synchronous activity – occurring for example during photostimulation – since the superimposition of multiple, co-occurring spike waveforms can make the detection of individual spikes difficult and unreliable (Roux et al., 2014; Stark et al., 2012).
evidence: This identifies a technical challenge with supporting citations.

claim: Obtaining ground truth validation of opto-tagging procedures is particularly challenging, especially in freely behaving animals.
source: While a number of strategies have been proposed for alleviating these problems (Roux et al., 2014; Royer et al., 2010; Stark et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2015), obtaining 'ground truth' validation of opto-tagging procedures is particularly challenging, especially in freely behaving animals.
evidence: This identifies a limitation of current methods with supporting citations.

claim: Opto-tagging approaches do not provide access to structural neuronal features like morphology and molecular expression patterns which are necessary for unequivocal cell-type identification.
source: A second important limitation is that opto-tagging approaches do not provide access to structural neuronal features – like for example morphology and molecular expression patterns – which are necessary for unequivocal cell-type identification.
evidence: This identifies a key limitation of optogenetic tagging methods.

claim: The combined opto-juxtacellular method enables targeting of juxtacellular recordings to a genetically predefined cell class, representing a significant advance over current juxtacellular protocols where individual neurons are blindly sampled.
source: This combination of techniques enables targeting of juxtacellular recordings to a genetically predefined cell class; hence, it represents a significant advance over current juxtacellular protocols, where individual neurons are blindly sampled within a target structure (Averkin et al., 2016; Diamantaki et al., 2018; Katona et al., 2014; Lapray et al., 2012; Tang et al., 2014a; Valero et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the advantage of the new method with citations to previous approaches.

claim: The juxtacellular opto-tagging approach could facilitate the targeting of sparse neuronal populations like different subtypes of GABAergic neurons.
source: This evidence indicates that our juxtacellular opto-tagging approach could facilitate the targeting of sparse neuronal populations – like different subtypes of GABAergic neurons (Bartos et al., 2011; Bartos and Elgueta, 2012; Klausberger, 2009; Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008)
evidence: This speculates on potential applications with supporting citations.

claim: Blind sampling of sparse neuronal populations in freely moving animals along with post hoc immunohistochemical phenotyping is known to be very challenging and labor intensive.
source: whose blind sampling in freely moving animals, along with post hoc immunohistochemical phenotyping, is known to be very challenging and labor intensive (Averkin et al., 2016; Katona et al., 2020; Lagler et al., 2016; Lapray et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating these challenges.

claim: The combined opto-juxtacellular method enables direct validation of opto-tagging criteria since single ChR2-responsive or nonresponsive neurons can be recorded and labeled by juxtacellular procedures, enabling post hoc verification of ChR2 and/or marker expression.
source: First, it enables direct validation of opto-tagging criteria, in that single ChR2-responsive (or nonresponsive) neurons can not only be recorded, but also labeled by juxtacellular procedures, thereby enabling post hoc verification of ChR2 and/or marker expression.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the new method.

claim: The large amplitude juxtacellular spikes (typically >1–2 mV peak-to-peak amplitudes) allow unequivocal spike identification, providing ground truth spiking signals that are not dependent on the performance of spike sorting algorithms.
source: Second, the large amplitude juxtacellular spikes (typically >1–2 mV peak-to-peak amplitudes, Herfst et al., 2012; Tang et al., 2014a) allow unequivocal spike identification, thereby providing 'ground truth' spiking signals that are not dependent on the performance of spike sorting algorithms, especially during photostimulation periods.
evidence: This describes an advantage of juxtacellular recordings with supporting citations.

claim: Post hoc morphological and molecular expression analysis of recorded/labeled cells provides access to structural features that are typically not accessible with alternative techniques, enabling unequivocal cell-type classification.
source: Third, post hoc morphological and molecular expression analysis of the recorded/labeled cells provides access to structural features that are typically not accessible with alternative techniques, thereby enabling unequivocal cell-type classification.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the juxtacellular labeling approach.

claim: The juxtacellular recording/labeling procedures can be used in combination with presynaptic input manipulations.
source: Moreover, our data also provide proof-of-principle evidence that our juxtacellular recording/labeling procedures can also be used in combination with presynaptic input manipulations (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes a capability demonstrated in Figure 2.

claim: The approach can be particularly useful for mapping synaptic inputs onto identified cell types like distinct subtypes of CA2 and CA3 pyramidal neurons or dentate granule cells.
source: This approach can be particularly useful for mapping synaptic inputs onto identified cell types, like for example the distinct subtypes of CA2 and CA3 pyramidal neurons (Helton et al., 2019; Hunt et al., 2018; Marissal et al., 2012; Raus Balind et al., 2019) or dentate granule cells (Diamantaki et al., 2016; Erwin et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020) which have been classified based on dendritic morphological criteria.
evidence: This speculates on potential applications with supporting citations.

claim: Future combination with single-cell stimulation will allow pairing between pre- and postsynaptic activity, enabling the study of single-cell plasticity mechanisms in the intact system during natural behaviors.
source: We envision that the future combination with single-cell stimulation (Diamantaki et al., 2018; Diamantaki et al., 2016), will allow pairing between pre- and postsynaptic activity (Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005; Salin et al., 1996; Toth et al., 2000), thus enabling the study of single-cell plasticity mechanisms, so far limited to simplified preparations, to the intact system during natural behaviors.
evidence: This speculates on future applications with supporting citations.

claim: The method remains laborious and of limited output compared to alternative techniques and should not be seen as high throughput but rather as complementary to existing in vivo recording methods.
source: While it is technically possible to perform multiple opto-juxtacellular recordings within individual experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), our method still remains laborious and of limited output compared to alternative techniques (e.g., extracellular recordings). Hence, it should not be seen as high throughput, but rather as complementary to existing in vivo recording methods.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations of the method.

claim: Opto-juxtacellular datasets could provide a valuable complement to current cell-type classification approaches by offering the possibility of building a classifier which could be used for assigning cell identity to blind extracellular units.
source: We envision that opto-juxtacellular datasets – although limited – could still provide a valuable complement to current cell-type classification approaches, for example by offering the possibility of building a classifier, which could then be used for assigning cell identity to 'blind' extracellular units (as in e.g. GoodSmith et al., 2017; Tang et al., 2014b).
evidence: This speculates on potential applications with supporting citations.

claim: Recent in vitro and in vivo work has shown that the CA1 pyramidal layer can be subdivided into two sublayers (superficial and deep) according to morphological, molecular, and electrophysiological criteria.
source: Recent in vitro and in vivo work has shown that the CA1 pyramidal layer can be subdivided into two sublayers (superficial and deep) according to morphological, molecular, and electrophysiological criteria (Baimbridge and Miller, 1982; Slomianka et al., 2011; Preston-Ferrer and Burgalossi, 2018; Soltesz and Losonczy, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on CA1 sublayers.

claim: Deep and superficial pyramidal cells have been shown to display distinct in vivo activity patterns relative to local field potential oscillations and distinct tendencies to express place fields.
source: Deep and superficial pyramidal cells have been shown to display distinct in vivo activity patterns relative to local field potential oscillations (Navas-Olive et al., 2020; Valero et al., 2015) and distinct tendencies to express place fields (Danielson et al., 2016; Geiller et al., 2017; Mizuseki et al., 2011; Navas-Olive et al., 2020; Sharif et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on CA1 pyramidal cell activity.

claim: Most previous in vivo observations on deep-superficial differences were based upon the anatomical assignment of extracellular recording locations.
source: However, most of the previous in vivo observations were based upon the anatomical assignment of extracellular recording locations (but see Valero et al., 2015; Navas-Olive et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the methodology of previous studies with citations.

claim: The study validated and extended previous observations by mapping functional deep-superficial gradients onto the underlying neuronal elements through recording, opto-tagging, and labeling single CA1 pyramidal neurons in freely moving mice.
source: As a testing ground for our technique, we recorded, opto-tagged, and labeled single CA1 pyramidal neurons in freely moving mice – thus validating and extending previous observations by mapping functional deep-superficial gradients onto the underlying neuronal elements.
evidence: This describes how the study extends previous work.

claim: Inputs from the medial and lateral entorhinal cortices are known to preferentially target deep and superficial CA1 pyramidal cells, respectively.
source: Notably, inputs from the medial and lateral entorhinal cortices are known to preferentially target deep and superficial CA1 pyramidal cells, respectively (Li et al., 2017; Masurkar et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The weaker spatial selectivity of upstream lateral entorhinal inputs might account for the weaker spatial tuning of Calb1-positive CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: hence, the weaker spatial selectivity of upstream lateral entorhinal inputs (Hargreaves et al., 2005) might account for the weaker spatial tuning of Calb1-positive CA1 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This proposes a mechanistic explanation with supporting citation.

claim: In Calb1cre mice injected within the CA1 pyramidal layer, ChR2 was almost exclusively expressed in Calb1-positive neurons (0 out of 272 neurons were ChR2-positive/Calb1-negative), confirming the specificity of the Calb1cre driver line.
source: In Calb1cre mice injected within the CA1 pyramidal layer, ChR2 was almost exclusively expressed in Calb1-positive neurons (0 out of 272 neurons were ChR2-positive/Calb1-negative), thus confirming the specificity of the Calb1cre driver line (see also Daigle et al., 2018; Nigro et al., 2018).
evidence: This reports validation data for the Cre driver line with supporting citations.

claim: Viral titers and injection volumes were optimized to obtain high infection efficiency and ChR2 expression levels (~95.8% of Calb1-positive neurons were also ChR2-positive; 261/272 neurons), minimizing the occurrence of false negatives in opto-tagging experiments.
source: Viral titers and injection volumes were optimized to obtain high infection efficiency and ChR2 expression levels (~95.8% of Calb1-positive neurons were also ChR2-positive; 261/272 neurons), thereby minimizing the occurrence of false negatives in our opto-tagging experiments.
evidence: This reports optimization of experimental parameters with quantitative data.

claim: For directly light-activated CA1 neurons, low-power intensities were sufficient for eliciting reliable spiking (typically <1 mW; range 0.1–1 mW).
source: For directly light-activated CA1 neurons, low-power intensities were sufficient for eliciting reliable spiking (typically <1 mW; range 0.1–1 mW).
evidence: This reports the light power requirements for direct activation.

claim: In the datasets of synaptically activated CA1 and CA3 neurons, higher light power (>1 mW; range 1–2.5 mW) was necessary for evoking spiking from light-responsive neurons, consistent with the notion that higher stimulus intensities are needed for synaptic activation compared to direct light activation.
source: In the datasets of synaptically activated CA1 and CA3 neurons (Figure 2), higher light power (>1 mW; range 1–2.5 mW) was necessary for evoking spiking from light-responsive neurons − consistent with the notion that higher stimulus intensities are needed for synaptic activation, as compared to direct light activation.
evidence: This reports light power requirements for synaptic activation with interpretation.

claim: In anesthetized animals, 5-ms light pulses largely evoked single spikes in responsive CA1 neurons (mean number of evoked spikes per pulse: 1.02 ± 0.04).
source: Notably, while in anesthetized animals, 5-ms light pulses largely evoked single spikes in the responsive CA1 neurons (mean number of evoked spikes per pulse, 1.02 ± 0.04)
evidence: This reports quantitative data on light-evoked responses in anesthetized animals.

claim: During awake behavior, 5-ms light pulses reliably evoked burst activity (i.e., 2–3 spikes at Interspike Intervals <6 ms).
source: during awake behavior, the same stimulation protocol reliably evoked burst activity (i.e., 2–3 spikes at Interspike Intervals (ISI) <6 ms; not shown).
evidence: This reports observations on light-evoked responses in awake animals.

claim: In order to elicit minimal light-evoked responses in the awake state, pulse duration was reduced to 1 ms (1 Hz frequency, 10–50 total pulses; mean number of evoked spikes per pulse: 1.56 ± 0.87).
source: In order to elicit minimal light-evoked responses in the awake state, pulse duration was thus reduced to 1 ms (1 Hz frequency, 10–50 total pulses; mean number of evoked spikes per pulse, 1.56 ± 0.87).
evidence: This reports the adjusted stimulation protocol for awake recordings with quantitative data.

claim: In a subset of anesthetized recordings (n = 4), putative Calb1-positive neurons could be reliably driven to spike with a 100-μm-core optic fiber coupled to a 470-nm LED light source.
source: In a subset of anesthetized recordings (n = 4), putative Calb1-positive neurons could also be reliably driven to spike with a 100-μm-core optic fiber, coupled to a 470-nm LED light source (M470F3, ThorLab).
evidence: This reports validation of the method with an alternative light source.

claim: Spike latencies with LED stimulation tended to be slightly longer than but not significantly different from spike latencies assessed with laser stimulation (laser: 2.45 ± 0.43 ms; LED: 2.96 ± 0.30 ms; p = 0.11).
source: Spike latencies tended to be slightly longer than – but not significantly different from – spike latencies assessed with laser stimulation (mean latencies; laser: 2.45 ± 0.43 ms; LED: 2.96 ± 0.30 ms; p = 0.11); hence, these recordings were pooled together.
evidence: This reports statistical comparison of latencies between light sources.

claim: A cell was defined as directly light activated (i.e., putative Calb1-positive) if short-latency spikes were evoked by the light stimulus (mean latency <4 ms).
source: A cell was defined as directly light activated (i.e., putative Calb1-positive) if short-latency spikes were evoked by the light stimulus (mean latency <4 ms).
evidence: This defines the classification criterion used in the study.

claim: ChR2-expressing neurons could be reliably entrained by the light stimuli up to 40 Hz frequencies.
source: ChR2-expressing neurons could be reliably entrained by the light stimuli up to 40 Hz frequencies (e.g., see Figure 1C, D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This reports the frequency response characteristics shown in figures.

claim: The dataset of directly light-activated CA1 recordings in anesthetized animals consisted of 10 Calb1-positive and 7 Calb1-negative pyramidal neurons from six mice.
source: The dataset of directly light-activated CA1 recordings in anesthetized animals (Figure 1; six mice) consisted of 10 Calb1-positive and 7 Calb1-negative pyramidal neurons (two additional recordings from putative Calb1-positive interneurons were excluded from further analysis, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C ).
evidence: This reports the composition of the anesthetized dataset.

claim: The datasets of indirect (synaptic) activation consisted of 7 light-activated CA3 cells from 4 mice and 11 light-activated CA1 cells from 3 mice.
source: The datasets of indirect (synaptic) activation consisted of 7 light-activated CA3 cells (4 mice) and 11 light-activated CA1 cells (3 mice) (Figure 2).
evidence: This reports the composition of the synaptic activation datasets.

claim: The dataset of CA1 recordings in freely moving animals (54 recordings) consisted of 10 recordings from histologically identified neurons and 44 recordings from opto-tagged neurons from 10 mice.
source: The dataset of CA1 recordings in freely moving animals (54 recordings) consisted of 10 recordings from histologically identified neurons (3 of which were reported in a previous study, Diamantaki et al., 2018) and 44 recordings from opto-tagged neurons (10 mice).
evidence: This reports the composition of the freely moving dataset with citation to previous work.

claim: Out of 10 histologically identified neurons in freely moving mice, 2 neurons were classified as Calb1-positive and 8 neurons were classified as Calb1-negative.
source: Out of the 10 histologically identified neurons, 2 neurons were classified as Calb1-positive and 8 neurons were classified as Calb1-negative (by Calbindin1 immunoreactivity and/or their relative position within the pyramidal layer, i.e., deep versus superficial).
evidence: This reports the classification of histologically identified neurons.

claim: Of the 44 opto-tagged recordings in freely moving mice, 13 were classified as putative Calb1-positive and 31 as putative Calb1-negative neurons based on spiking probability and spike latency to the light stimulus.
source: Of the 44 opto-tagged recordings, 13 were classified as putative Calb1-positive and 31 as putative Calb1-negative neurons, based on spiking probability and spike latency to the light stimulus (see Figure 3B and main text).
evidence: This reports the classification of opto-tagged neurons.

claim: For the analysis of spatial firing patterns, 38 of 54 recordings met the inclusion criteria (>50 spikes and ≥3 laps), consisting of 12 putative Calb1-positive and 26 putative Calb1-negative neurons.
source: For the analysis of spatial firing patterns (spatial information per spike, sparsity, and spatial stability, Figure 3K and Figure 3—figure supplement 2) a speed threshold was applied (speed >1 cm/s) and only recordings with >50 spikes and ≥3 laps were included. In total, 38 of 54 recordings met these inclusion criteria (12 putative Calb1-positive and 26 putative Calb1-negative neurons, see Figure 3I–K).
evidence: This reports the sample size and inclusion criteria for spatial analysis.

claim: Applying more stringent inclusion criteria (e.g., >3 laps, >100 spikes) and/or different speed thresholds (1–10 cm/s) led to qualitatively similar results and did not change the statistical significance of the findings (P < 0.05).
source: Applying more stringent inclusion criteria (e.g., >3 laps, > 100 spikes) and/or different speed thresholds (1–10 cm/s) led to qualitatively similar results and did not change the statistical significance of our findings (P < 0.05 for Figure 3I–K).
evidence: This reports robustness analysis of the main findings.
